text.p: Rumors that the investment bank Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc may be swallowed up by a New York commercial bank swept Wall Street Wednesday, and although none of the parties was willing to comment, analysts and traders said a deal could not be ruled out.

One trader, asked if either Chase Manhattan Corp or J.P. Morgan & Co Inc could be potential buyers considering that both have been building up their investment banking internally, used a baseball analogy.

"It's like George Steinbrenner and the Yankees," he said. He observed that while the Yankees have a minor league farm team system, owner Steinbrenner "is always paying big bucks to get players from the other major league teams."

Asked to assess Chase Manhattan's internal efforts to build investment banking, one analyst said "I think it's been very successful. They have attracted a number of very well known people from Salomon Brothers and a number of places." The analyst asked not to be identified.
Another rumored acquirer was the Dutch financial services giant Internationale Nederlanden Groep NV. ING could not immediately be reached for comment.

The rumors found fertile ground and sent Lehman's stock rocketing 3-7/8 to close at 38, after being up as much as 7-7/8 during the day. A spokesman for Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc declined comment on the rumors, citing company policy.

Two deals announced earlier this year have triggered a torrent of speculation about "me too" deals. First, main street broker Dean Witter Discover & Co agreed to merge with blue blood investment bank Morgan Stanley Group Inc.

Then Bankers Trust New York Corp agreed to buy broker Alex. Brown Inc. Although Bankers Trust chairman and chief executive Frank Newman refers to Bankers Trust as a capital markets firm rather than a bank, it is still strictly speaking a bank buying a broker.

In the weeks following those deals, several Wall Street chieftains said that it was unfair that under U.S. securities laws a bank can buy a broker, but a broker could buy only a small piece of a bank.

Merrill Lynch & Co chairman and chief executive David Komansky said the rules were not fair, and PaineWebber Group Inc chairman and chief executive Donald Marron agreed. Sanford Weill, chairman and chief executive of Travelers Group Inc and a veteran of many Wall Street deals, said the rules now in place are "not the American way."
A trader who did not want to be identified said the banks are hungry to get into the lucrative world of initial public offerings (IPOs) of stock and secondary offerings.

Raphael Soifer, an analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman, was somewhat skeptical about the rumors. "I would say it's rather unlikely," he said, referring to either Chase Manhattan or J.P. Morgan buying Lehman. But he added the caveat, "we have all learned not to say 'never.' Stranger things have happened."

Soifer said J.P. Morgan, which has not made a big acquisition since it bought Guaranty Trust in 1959, is in its own right a "bulge bracket" firm in fixed income. Fixed income is the strength of Lehman.
Chase, in its public comments, has been talking about building internally, Soifer said.
